subject: Social Science
chapter: History: The Rise of Nationalism in Europe
text: Nationalism spread in 19th-century Europe. The French Revolution (1789) introduced ideas of the nation, sovereignty of the people, and symbols like the tricolour and La Marseillaise. Napoleon's Civil Code (1804) removed feudal privileges and brought uniform laws, though he also curtailed freedoms. A 'nation-state' formed where citizens shared a common identity. The liberal middle class demanded freedom and constitutions; the Congress of Vienna (1815) restored conservative monarchies. Romanticism used art, poetry, and folk culture to build national feeling. Unification of Germany (led by Prussia's Bismarck through wars) and Italy (Mazzini's 'Young Italy', Cavour, Garibaldi) completed nation-building. Britain's nation formed gradually (Act of Union 1707). The allegory of the nation was shown as female figures like Marianne (France) and Germania. The Balkans became a region of intense nationalist conflict.

subject: Social Science
text: Indian nationalism grew against colonial rule. The First World War, high taxes, and the Rowlatt Act (1919) caused anger; the Jallianwala Bagh massacre (1919) shocked the nation. Gandhi introduced Satyagraha (truth and non-violence). The Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-22) called for boycott of schools, foreign goods, and titles, but was withdrawn after the Chauri Chaura incident. The Civil Disobedience Movement began with the Dandi Salt March (1930), breaking the salt law. Different groups joined: peasants, tribals, workers, women, and the business class, though with varied hopes. The idea of 'Bharat Mata' and folklore, flags, and songs built unity. The movement had limits (Dr Ambedkar's concerns for Dalits, Muslim League's separate demands). It culminated in the demand for Purna Swaraj (complete independence).

subject: Social Science
chapter: History: The Making of a Global World
text: Globalisation has a long history. In the pre-modern world, trade, migration, and the movement of goods, people, and ideas connected regions (e.g. the Silk Routes). Foods like potatoes, maize, and chillies spread across continents after Columbus reached the Americas. Disease (like smallpox) enabled European conquest of the Americas. In the 19th century, three flows linked the world: trade (goods), labour (migration), and capital (investment). The 'Corn Laws' in Britain and indentured labour migration (from India) shaped economies. The rinderpest cattle plague devastated Africa. The World Wars and the Great Depression (1929) disrupted the global economy. After WWII, the Bretton Woods institutions (IMF and World Bank) were set up to rebuild and stabilise the post-war economy, beginning modern globalisation.

subject: Social Science
text: Before factories, 'proto-industrialisation' involved production by hand in homes for merchants. The Industrial Revolution in Britain began with cotton and the textile industry; inventions and steam power (James Watt) mechanised production in factories. Early factories brought harsh conditions, child labour, and low wages. In India, colonial rule harmed traditional industries: cheap British machine-made cloth flooded markets, ruining weavers, while Indian raw materials were exported. Later, Indian entrepreneurs set up industries (e.g. early cotton mills, jute). Industrial growth was uneven; small-scale and handicraft production survived alongside factories. Advertisements and labels were used to sell goods and build markets. Industrialisation transformed work, cities, and society.

subject: Social Science
chapter: History: Print Culture and the Modern World
text: Print technology began in China, Japan, and Korea (woodblock print). Gutenberg developed the first printing press in Europe (around 1450), making the Bible the first printed book. The print revolution lowered book costs, spread literacy, and enabled the circulation of ideas — fuelling the Reformation, the Enlightenment, and the French Revolution. It created a 'reading public' and public debate. In India, print came with missionaries; newspapers, journals, and books in Indian languages spread reform ideas, nationalism, and awareness (e.g. Raja Rammohun Roy's writings, novels, and periodicals for women and the poor). Print helped reform movements and the freedom struggle but was also controlled through colonial censorship (e.g. Vernacular Press Act, 1878).

subject: Social Science
text: A resource is anything in the environment that can satisfy human needs and is technologically accessible, economically feasible, and culturally acceptable. Classification: by origin (biotic, abiotic), exhaustibility (renewable, non-renewable), ownership (individual, community, national, international), and status of development (potential, developed, stock, reserve). Sustainable development means meeting present needs without compromising future generations; the Rio Earth Summit (1992) and Agenda 21 promote it. Resource planning is essential in India due to uneven distribution. Land use: land is a natural resource used for agriculture, forests, pasture, and settlement. Soil is a renewable natural resource; types include alluvial, black (regur, for cotton), red and yellow, laterite, arid, and forest soils. Soil erosion (by water, wind) is prevented by contour ploughing, terrace farming, strip cropping, and shelter belts.

subject: Social Science
text: India has rich biodiversity (flora and fauna) but faces threats. The IUCN classifies species as normal, endangered, vulnerable, rare, endemic, and extinct. Causes of depletion: expansion of agriculture, mining, developmental projects, and grazing. Conservation preserves ecological diversity and the gene pool. India's Wildlife Protection Act (1972) protects species and habitats; Project Tiger (1973) and reserves protect key animals. Types of forests by ownership/management: Reserved forests (most valuable, protected), Protected forests, and Unclassed forests. Community and local participation (e.g. Chipko movement, sacred groves, Joint Forest Management) plays a vital role in conservation.

subject: Social Science
text: Water is a renewable resource, but freshwater is limited, causing water scarcity due to overuse, population growth, industrialisation, and pollution. Multipurpose river projects and dams provide irrigation, electricity (hydropower), water supply, and flood control (e.g. Bhakra-Nangal, Hirakud), but cause problems: displacement of people, submerging of forests, and ecological changes (movements like the Narmada Bachao Andolan protest these). Rainwater harvesting is a traditional and sustainable method to conserve water (e.g. tankas in Rajasthan, rooftop harvesting, guls/kuls in the hills, tanks in the south). Conservation and management of water are essential for sustainability.

subject: Social Science
text: Agriculture is the primary occupation of most Indians. Farming types: primitive subsistence (slash-and-burn), intensive subsistence (high labour, small plots), and commercial (for market, uses HYV seeds, fertilisers). Cropping seasons: Rabi (winter, e.g. wheat, gram), Kharif (monsoon, e.g. rice, maize, cotton), and Zaid (summer, e.g. watermelon). Major crops: rice, wheat, millets (jowar, bajra, ragi), pulses, sugarcane, oilseeds, tea, coffee, and horticulture; fibre crops include cotton and jute. Government reforms: land reforms, the Green Revolution, and support (MSP, subsidies). Food security and the impact of globalisation on Indian agriculture are important concerns.

subject: Social Science
text: A mineral is a naturally occurring homogeneous substance. Types: metallic (ferrous like iron ore, manganese; non-ferrous like copper, bauxite), non-metallic (limestone, mica), and energy minerals (coal, petroleum). Minerals occur in veins, lodes, beds, and placer deposits. Conservation is vital as minerals are exhaustible and take ages to form. Energy resources: conventional (coal, petroleum, natural gas, electricity — thermal and hydro) and non-conventional (solar, wind, tidal, geothermal, biogas, nuclear). India promotes renewable energy for sustainability. Overuse and pollution from fossil fuels make conservation and clean energy essential.

subject: Social Science
text: Manufacturing means producing goods in large quantities from raw materials; it is part of the secondary sector and boosts the economy. Importance: creates jobs, reduces dependence on agriculture, and earns foreign exchange. Classification: by raw material (agro-based like textiles, sugar; mineral-based like iron and steel), by role (basic and consumer), by capital, and by ownership (public, private, joint, cooperative). Key industries: textiles (cotton, jute), iron and steel (needs iron ore, coal, limestone), aluminium, cement, automobiles, and IT. Industrial location depends on raw materials, power, labour, market, and transport. Industries cause air, water, land, and noise pollution; control measures and sustainable practices are needed.

subject: Social Science
text: Transport and communication are lifelines linking production and consumption. Roadways (India has a large network; national highways, expressways) are flexible and door-to-door. Railways are the principal mode for long-distance freight and passengers. Pipelines transport crude oil, gas, and water. Waterways (inland and shipping) are the cheapest; major ports handle overseas trade. Airways are the fastest but costliest. Communication: personal (post, telephone) and mass (radio, TV, newspaper, internet). International trade (imports and exports) reflects a country's economic development; tourism is also a service that earns foreign exchange and creates jobs.

subject: Social Science
text: Power-sharing is the distribution of power among different organs and levels of government and social groups. Case studies: Belgium (accommodated ethnic Dutch, French, and German speakers through a careful power-sharing arrangement) and Sri Lanka (majoritarianism where the Sinhala majority dominated, alienating Tamils and leading to civil conflict). Reasons for power-sharing: prudential (avoids conflict, ensures stability) and moral (the spirit of democracy is sharing power with those affected). Forms of power-sharing: (1) horizontal (among legislature, executive, judiciary — checks and balances), (2) vertical (among central, state, and local governments), (3) among different social groups (community government), and (4) among political parties, pressure groups, and movements.

subject: Social Science
text: Federalism is a system where power is divided between a central authority and constituent units (states). Features: two or more levels of government, each with its own jurisdiction, guaranteed by a written constitution, with the courts settling disputes. India is a federation with three tiers: Union, State, and Local government. The Constitution divides subjects into the Union List, State List, and Concurrent List (residuary powers with the Centre). Language policy (no national language; scheduled languages; Hindi and English for official use) and Centre-State financial relations support federalism. Decentralisation: the 1992 constitutional amendment created a strong third tier — Panchayati Raj (rural) and Municipalities (urban) — with elections, reservations for women and weaker sections, giving power to local people.

subject: Social Science
chapter: Political Science: Gender, Religion and Caste
text: Social divisions based on gender, religion, and caste influence politics. Gender: the sexual division of labour and gender inequality led to the feminist movement; women's political representation is still low (reservation in local bodies helps). Religion in politics: communalism (using religion for political dominance) is dangerous; a secular state (India) gives no state religion and equal treatment to all faiths, with freedom of religion as a fundamental right. Caste: caste inequality persists; caste can shape voting and politics ('casteism'), but no single caste wins elections alone. Politics and these divisions influence each other; healthy democracy addresses inequalities rather than exploiting divisions.

subject: Social Science
text: A political party is a group that contests elections and holds power, with an ideology, a leadership, and members. Functions: contest elections, form policies and programmes, make laws, form and run governments, act as opposition, shape public opinion, and provide access to welfare schemes. Party systems: one-party, two-party, and multi-party (India has a multi-party system). Types: national parties (recognised nationwide) and state (regional) parties. Challenges: lack of internal democracy, dynastic succession, money and muscle power, and the lack of meaningful choice. Reforms: anti-defection law, disclosure of assets by candidates, and regulation by the Election Commission strengthen parties and democracy.

subject: Social Science
text: Democracy is judged by its outcomes. Expected outcomes: (1) Accountable, responsive, and legitimate government — democracy produces a government that follows procedures, is open to public scrutiny, and is accepted as people's own. (2) Economic growth and development — democracies have a mixed record, but they are preferable given their other benefits. (3) Reduction of inequality and poverty — a challenge, as economic inequalities persist. (4) Accommodation of social diversity — democracy handles differences and conflicts peacefully. (5) Dignity and freedom of citizens — democracy promotes equality and individual dignity (e.g. for women and the marginalised). Democracy is better than other forms because it allows correction of its own mistakes.

subject: Social Science
text: Development means different things to different people; it involves both income and non-material goals (equal treatment, freedom, security, respect). National development considers the goals of many. Income comparison of countries uses per capita income (average income), used by the World Bank to classify rich and low-income countries. But income alone is not enough; other indicators matter: health (life expectancy, infant mortality rate), education (literacy rate, net attendance ratio), and living standards. The UNDP's Human Development Index (HDI) combines income, education, and health to rank countries. Sustainability of development is crucial — resources must be used so that future generations' needs are not harmed (e.g. groundwater depletion, non-renewable resources).

subject: Social Science
chapter: Economics: Sectors of the Indian Economy
text: The economy has three sectors: primary (agriculture, mining — natural products), secondary (industry, manufacturing), and tertiary (services — transport, banking, trade). Sectors are also classified as organised (regular, secure jobs with benefits, follows rules) and unorganised (irregular, low-paid, no security) and as public (government-owned, aims at welfare) and private (privately owned, aims at profit). In India, over time the tertiary sector has become the largest contributor to GDP, but most people still work in agriculture, showing underemployment (disguised unemployment). GDP is the value of all final goods and services produced. Schemes like MGNREGA (right to work) support the unorganised sector. Protecting workers in the unorganised sector is important.

subject: Social Science
text: Money is a medium of exchange that removes the problem of the double coincidence of wants (in barter). Modern forms: currency (notes and coins, issued by the RBI) and deposits in banks (demand deposits, usable by cheque). Banks accept deposits and lend, keeping only a fraction as reserves. Credit (loans) can help (expand business, farming) or trap people in a debt cycle if terms are unfavourable. Loans need collateral (an asset the borrower owns) and have terms of credit (interest rate, collateral, documentation, mode of repayment). Two sources of credit: formal (banks, cooperatives — regulated by RBI, lower interest) and informal (moneylenders, traders — high interest, no supervision). Self-Help Groups (SHGs) help poor, especially women, get affordable credit and promote saving.

subject: Social Science
chapter: Economics: Globalisation and the Indian Economy
text: Globalisation is the integration of economies through the rapid flow of goods, services, investment, technology, and people across countries. Multinational Corporations (MNCs) produce goods and services in multiple countries, investing where it is cheap and profitable, connecting distant markets. Factors enabling globalisation: rapid improvement in technology (transport, IT, the internet), and the liberalisation of trade and investment (removal of barriers like tariffs). In India, liberalisation began around 1991. The WTO promotes free trade, though rules often favour developed nations. Impacts: consumers get more choice and quality; some producers and workers benefit while others face tough competition. A fair globalisation with government support for the weak is needed.

subject: Social Science
text: Consumers can be exploited through underweighing, overcharging, adulteration, false information, and defective goods. The consumer movement arose to protect buyers. Consumer rights: right to safety, right to be informed (e.g. details on labels, expiry, MRP), right to choose, right to seek redressal, right to represent, and the right to consumer education. Standard marks assure quality: ISI (industrial goods), Agmark (agricultural products), Hallmark (gold). The Consumer Protection Act (COPRA), 1986 set up a three-tier system of consumer courts (District, State, and National) for redressal. RTI (Right to Information) empowers citizens. Consumer awareness (Jago Grahak Jago) and responsible buying help protect rights.
